name: Dumbbell bench press
form_cue: Elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso, not flared to 90. Press until your arms are straight but not locked hard.
why: The primary horizontal press for a home dumbbell setup - chest, shoulders, and triceps all load together.

name: Barbell bench press
form_cue: Bar over your wrists, shoulder blades pinned back and down into the bench, feet flat and driving into the floor the whole rep.
why: Heaviest load you can safely put through a horizontal press - the anchor chest lift once you've got a rack and a spotter or safety pins.

name: Push-up
form_cue: Straight line head to heel, full range down to your chest nearly touching the floor, elbows track back at roughly 45 degrees.
why: No-equipment horizontal push that scales from knees to feet to a weighted vest - covers a huge range before anything else is needed.

name: Dumbbell fly
form_cue: Slight bend in the elbow held constant through the rep, lower until you feel a stretch across the chest, squeeze back to the top without banging the dumbbells together.
why: Isolates the chest through a longer stretch than a press can, which is where a lot of chest growth actually happens.

name: Cable fly
form_cue: Slight forward lean, arms sweep in a wide arc down and together in front of your chest, control the return - don't let the weight stack yank your arms back.
why: Cable keeps tension on the chest through the whole range, including the stretched bottom position a dumbbell fly loses.

name: Dumbbell overhead press
form_cue: Brace your core hard before you press - don't let your lower back arch to get the weight up.
why: Overhead strength and shoulder stability that a lower-body-focused program tends to neglect.

name: Barbell overhead press
form_cue: Bar starts at your collarbone, brace and press straight up, tuck your head through once the bar clears your face.
why: The heaviest overhead press variant available once a rack is on hand - builds shoulder strength that carries into every overhead reach.

name: Pike push-up
form_cue: Hips high, forming an inverted V, lower the crown of your head toward the floor between your hands, press back up through the shoulders.
why: Bodyweight overhead press substitute and the standard first step on the road to a handstand push-up.

name: Dumbbell lateral raise
form_cue: Slight bend in the elbows, raise to shoulder height leading with the elbows not the hands, stop before the shoulders shrug up.
why: Isolates the side delt directly - the part of the shoulder that gives width and is easiest to underload with pressing alone.

name: Band lateral raise
form_cue: Stand on the band, slight elbow bend, raise to shoulder height and control the band back down - don't let it snap your arm to your side.
why: Same side-delt target as a dumbbell raise, useful when the lightest dumbbell you own is already too heavy for strict form here.

name: Dumbbell overhead triceps extension
form_cue: Elbows pointed forward and pinned close to your ears, lower the dumbbell behind your head under control, extend back up without flaring the elbows out.
why: Direct triceps isolation through the long head, which a pressing exercise alone under-trains.

name: Cable triceps pushdown
form_cue: Elbows pinned to your sides the whole rep, push the bar down until your arms are straight, let it rise only to about 90 degrees.
why: Constant cable tension on the triceps with almost no technique cost - an easy accessory to add real volume with.

name: Bench dip
form_cue: Hands on the bench edge behind you, lower until your elbows hit about 90 degrees, keep your shoulders down away from your ears.
why: No-equipment triceps builder that also loads the chest and front delts - a natural step before bar dips.

name: Bar dips
form_cue: Lean forward slightly, lower until your shoulders drop below your elbows, press back up without flaring the elbows wide.
why: The full-range calisthenics dip - heavier loading on chest, shoulders, and triceps than a bench dip can give once bodyweight gets easy.

name: Single-arm dumbbell row
form_cue: Flat back braced on the bench, pull the dumbbell to your hip, elbow brushing your ribs, don't let your torso rotate to help it up.
why: Matches pressing volume with pulling volume one side at a time, which also catches any left-right imbalance a barbell row can hide.

name: Barbell row
form_cue: Hinge to roughly 45 degrees, flat back, pull the bar to your lower ribs and lower it under control - don't let your hips rise on the pull.
why: Heaviest back-thickness builder available once you've got a bar - the bilateral equivalent of the dumbbell row.

name: Band row
form_cue: Anchor the band at chest height, sit or stand tall, pull your elbows straight back and squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end.
why: A rowing option that needs nothing but a door anchor - keeps pulling volume in the plan on a trip or a no-dumbbells day.

name: Pull-up
form_cue: Full hang at the bottom, chin clears the bar at the top, control the descent rather than dropping.
why: The benchmark vertical pull and the single best back-width movement bodyweight training has - everything else in the pull-up family builds toward this.

name: Band-assisted pull-up
form_cue: Loop the band over the bar and under your foot or knee. Full hang at the bottom, chin clears the bar at the top, control the descent.
why: Takes just enough load off a pull-up to practice the full range with good form while strict strength is still building.

name: Negative pull-up
form_cue: Jump or step up to the top position, chin over the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can - aim for a 5 second count down.
why: Eccentric strength builds faster than concentric - often the fastest route from zero pull-ups to the first unassisted rep.

name: Lat pulldown
form_cue: Lean back slightly, pull the bar to your upper chest leading with your elbows, control it back up to a full stretch.
why: Trains the same vertical pull pattern as a pull-up with a dialed-in load, useful for building the strength base a first pull-up needs.

name: Dumbbell biceps curl
form_cue: Elbows pinned to your sides the whole rep, curl without swinging your torso, lower all the way to a straight arm.
why: Direct biceps work that a compound pull doesn't fully cover - keeps elbow flexion strong for grip-heavy pulling.

name: Band biceps curl
form_cue: Stand on the band, elbows pinned to your sides, curl up under control and resist the band on the way down instead of letting it snap you back.
why: Keeps the same biceps isolation available with nothing but a band, for a no-dumbbells day.

name: Barbell curl
form_cue: Elbows pinned to your sides, curl the bar up without leaning back to help it, lower all the way under control.
why: The heaviest biceps isolation option - lets both arms move the same bar together once a barbell is on hand.

name: Goblet squat
form_cue: Hold a dumbbell vertically at your chest, sit back and down between your heels, chest stays tall the whole way.
why: The front-loaded position naturally keeps your torso upright, which makes this the easiest squat pattern to teach and to load safely at home.

name: Barbell back squat
form_cue: Bar sits across your upper back, brace before you descend, hips and chest drop together - don't let your chest cave forward first.
why: The heaviest lower-body lift a rack allows and the anchor squat once goblet loads stop being enough.

name: Bodyweight squat
form_cue: Feet shoulder width, sit back and down until your thighs are at least parallel, knees track over your toes.
why: The no-equipment version of the pattern - warms up the same hip and knee mechanics before anything gets loaded on top.

name: Bulgarian split squat
form_cue: Back foot elevated on a bench, dumbbells at your sides, drop straight down until the back knee nearly grazes the floor.
why: Closes the gap between your dominant and non-dominant leg - a bilateral squat alone can't catch a side-to-side imbalance.

name: Bodyweight split squat
form_cue: Long stride, back heel lifted, drop the back knee straight down toward the floor and drive back up through the front foot.
why: Single-leg strength and balance with no equipment needed - the entry point before adding dumbbells or a rear-foot elevation.

name: Dumbbell step-up
form_cue: Bench or box at about knee height, drive through the planted heel to stand tall - don't push off the trailing foot.
why: Direct single-leg power that carries straight into running, jumping, and change-of-direction sports.

name: Bodyweight step-up
form_cue: Full foot on the step before you drive up, control the descent back down instead of just stepping off.
why: Same single-leg step pattern with no load needed - useful as a warm-up rehearsal or for anyone new to single-leg work.

name: Barbell deadlift
form_cue: Bar over your midfoot, flat back, push the floor away with your legs while the bar stays close to your shins the whole way up.
why: The heaviest full-body hinge available and the clearest single test of posterior chain strength there is.

name: Dumbbell Romanian deadlift
form_cue: Push hips back first, soft knee bend, dumbbells trace close down your legs. Stop the descent when your lower back wants to round.
why: The primary posterior chain lift for a home dumbbell setup - hamstrings, glutes, and spinal control all get built here.

name: Bodyweight good morning
form_cue: Hands behind your head, soft knees, hinge forward from the hips until you feel your hamstrings, stand back up.
why: Rehearses the hip hinge pattern with no load - the standard warm-up before any loaded hinge like an RDL or deadlift.

name: Barbell hip thrust
form_cue: Upper back braced on a bench, bar across your hips, drive through your heels until your hips are fully extended and your ribs stay down.
why: Trains the glutes through end-range hip extension at a heavier load than any hinge or squat variant can put on them directly.

name: Dumbbell hip thrust
form_cue: Upper back braced on a bench, dumbbell held across your hips, drive through your heels to full hip extension and squeeze at the top.
why: Same end-range glute loading as a barbell hip thrust, scaled to a home dumbbell setup.

name: Glute bridge
form_cue: Feet flat, knees bent, drive your hips up until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, squeeze the glutes at the top.
why: The no-equipment entry point into hip extension - also the standard glute activation drill ahead of a squat or a skill session.

name: Single-leg glute bridge
form_cue: One foot planted, the other leg extended straight, drive through the planted heel and keep your hips level - don't let the free side dip.
why: Forces one glute to fire on its own, which a two-leg bridge lets a weaker side hide behind. The standard fix when one side tests behind the other on a single-leg skill.

name: Front plank
form_cue: Elbows under your shoulders, straight line from head to heel, squeeze your glutes so your hips don't sag.
why: Baseline anti-extension core hold - the entry point every other plank variant scales up from.

name: Side plank
form_cue: Stack your feet, prop up on one elbow directly under your shoulder, lift your hips until your body forms a straight line.
why: Trains the obliques and lateral hip stabilizers that a front plank doesn't reach - directly protects against side-to-side collapse under load.

name: Weighted plank
form_cue: Same setup as a front plank with a plate or dumbbell placed flat across your upper back, brace hard so your hips don't sag under the extra load.
why: Once a bodyweight plank holds well past a minute, added load is what keeps the hold genuinely challenging instead of just longer.

name: Band Pallof press
form_cue: Band anchored to your side at chest height, press it straight out in front of you and hold - resist letting your torso rotate toward the anchor.
why: Anti-rotation strength that carries directly into any sport with a swing or a twist - badminton smashes and cricket bowling both load this exact pattern.

name: Cable woodchop
form_cue: Pivot your back foot and rotate through your torso, not just your arms, pulling the cable from high to low across your body.
why: Trains rotational power under load rather than just resisting rotation - useful once anti-rotation holds get easy.

name: Dead bug
form_cue: Lower back pressed flat into the floor the entire rep, extend the opposite arm and leg slowly, stop the moment your back wants to arch off the floor.
why: Teaches your core to resist your lower back arching under load - the exact fault a heavy hinge or press exposes first.

name: Weighted dead bug
form_cue: Hold a light dumbbell overhead with both hands. Lower back stays flat on the floor. Extend the opposite leg slow.
why: Adds real anti-extension load once the bodyweight version stops being challenging - protects the lower back on every heavy hinge and press in a program.

name: Standing calf raise
form_cue: Rise onto the balls of your feet as high as you can, pause at the top, lower under control past level if you're on a step.
why: Direct calf strength that supports every running and jumping stride - easy to underload since bodyweight alone gets easy fast.

name: Standing calf raise, dumbbells
form_cue: Hold a dumbbell in each hand, rise onto the balls of your feet, pause at the top and lower slowly.
why: Adds load once bodyweight calf raises stop being enough - keeps calf strength progressing alongside the rest of the leg.

name: Seated calf raise
form_cue: Knees bent under the pad, rise onto the balls of your feet through a full range, pause and lower slowly.
why: Targets the soleus specifically with the knee bent, which a standing raise trains less directly - fills out complete calf development.

name: Strict pull-up
form_cue: Dead hang start, pull until your chin clears the bar, lower back to a full hang under control - no kipping.
why: The skill-tracked endpoint of the pull-up family - once this is clean for real sets, the next step is adding weight, not more reps.

name: Weighted pull-up
form_cue: Belt or vest loaded, same dead-hang-to-chin-over-bar range as a bodyweight pull-up - don't shorten the range to handle the added weight.
why: Progressive overload on a movement bodyweight reps alone can no longer challenge.

name: Wall handstand hold
form_cue: Chest to the wall, stack shoulders over wrists, squeeze your glutes and brace your core so your lower back doesn't arch.
why: Builds the shoulder strength and body line of a handstand with the wall taking away the balance problem, so you can train the strength piece on its own.

name: Freestanding handstand hold
form_cue: Kick up with control, find your balance point over your wrists using small finger presses, not a big hip break.
why: The full skill once the wall hold and shoulder strength are solid - balance is the last piece, and it only comes from practicing away from the wall.

name: Tuck front lever hold
form_cue: Hang from the bar, pull your knees to your chest and roll your hips under until your back is parallel to the floor, keep your arms straight.
why: The entry-level lever position - builds the straight-arm pulling strength every longer lever variant needs before the legs extend.

name: Single-leg front lever hold
form_cue: One leg extended straight in line with your torso, the other tucked to your chest, hips level - keep the extended-leg glute actively squeezed so that side doesn't sag.
why: The bridge step between tuck and full front lever - extending one leg at a time surfaces a left-right strength gap a two-leg hold can hide.

name: Full front lever hold
form_cue: Body fully extended and parallel to the floor, arms straight, squeeze your glutes and brace your core the entire hold.
why: The full expression of the skill - both legs extended with no tuck to hide behind, straight-arm back and core strength at its highest demand.

name: Standing glute activation hinge
form_cue: Hands on hips, push your hips straight back then squeeze forward to standing, cue the glute to finish the movement rather than the lower back.
why: A tight or under-firing glute shows up as an activation fault, not a strength deficit - this wakes it up before the session, not under a skill load where it's harder to fix.

name: Band lateral walk
form_cue: Band around your ankles or above your knees, stay in a quarter-squat, step sideways keeping tension on the band the whole time - don't let your feet drift together.
why: Direct hip abductor and glute medius work, the muscles that keep the knee tracking straight on every step and squat.

name: 90/90 hip stretch
form_cue: Sit with the front leg bent 90 degrees in front of you and the back leg bent 90 degrees behind, lean your chest gently over the front shin.
why: Standard release for a tight hip - hold on the tighter side longer, and don't load a tight glute before releasing it first.

name: Band external rotation
form_cue: Anchor the band at waist height. Elbow bent 90 degrees, pinned to your side, rotate the forearm outward only - the elbow doesn't move.
why: Strengthens the infraspinatus and teres minor - the rotator cuff muscles that decelerate the arm on every overhead swing, throw, or smash.

name: Band internal rotation
form_cue: Same elbow-pinned setup as external rotation, rotate the forearm inward across your body, slow and controlled on the way back.
why: Balances the external rotation work - a shoulder strong in one rotational direction and weak in the other is an injury pattern waiting to happen.

name: Band Y-raise
form_cue: Slight forward lean, arms form a Y at 45 degrees, thumbs up, raise to shoulder height only.
why: Targets the lower trapezius specifically - weak here is one of the most common drivers of shoulder impingement in overhead athletes.

name: Chin tuck
form_cue: Sitting tall, glide your head straight back like making a double chin, don't tilt up or down.
why: Directly retrains forward head posture - one of the most common and least-addressed desk postural faults.

name: Prone cobra
form_cue: Face down, arms at your sides, lift your chest and squeeze your shoulder blades together and down, thumbs point up.
why: Builds endurance in the upper back extensors that fight gravity all day to keep you upright - bodyweight but genuinely hard when done right.

name: Band pull-apart
form_cue: Arms straight, pull the band apart to touch your chest, squeeze your shoulder blades hard at the end range.
why: Directly activates the mid-trapezius and rhomboids - the muscles that pull rounded shoulders back into a neutral position.
